title: Creating Optical Illusions
sub: Art Meets Science · Grades 5–8 · Art · 30 minutes
objective: Students will analyze how artists use perspective, color theory, and pattern to create optical illusions, study examples from the Op Art movement and M.C. Escher, and create their own optical illusion artwork.
materials: White drawing paper, rulers, compasses, pencils, erasers
Colored pencils, markers, or fine-tip pens
Examples: M.C. Escher works (*Waterfall*, *Ascending and Descending*, *Relativity*)
Examples: Op Art (Bridget Riley, Victor Vasarely)
Recommended from Perception Lab: Impossible Trident (#15), Café Wall (#6), Fraser Spiral (#5), Bulging Grid (#7)
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the Mini Museum:** The Victorian optical illusion cards use similar techniques—transformation cards revealing hidden images, patterns that seem to move. The stereoscope creates depth from flat images.

**Option 2 — Virtual Visit:** Show the exhibition online at *minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving* or view artifacts at *minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving/artifacts*

steps.title: Trace the water
script: Display M.C. Escher’s *Waterfall* (water appears to flow uphill in an impossible loop).

*“At first glance, this looks normal. But trace the path of the water with your finger. Where does it go?”* Let students discover the impossibility. *“This is an ‘impossible object’—something that can exist in 2D but never in real life. Dutch artist M.C. Escher was a master at these.”*

steps.purpose: Let students discover the impossibility for themselves.

steps.title: Is it moving?
script: Show a Bridget Riley Op Art piece (black and white patterns that appear to move).
*“This painting isn’t moving—but your brain thinks it is! This is Op Art, short for ‘optical art.’ Artists in the 1960s deliberately created works that trick your visual system.”*

steps.title: Three illusion techniques
script: **Impossible objects** — **What:** Shapes that look 3D but violate geometry **How:** Local parts look correct, but whole is impossible **Artists:** M.C. Escher, Oscar Reutersvärd (invented impossible triangle, 1934)

**Op Art patterns** — **What:** Geometric patterns creating movement, depth, vibration **How:** High-contrast repetitive patterns overwhelm visual processing **Artists:** Bridget Riley, Victor Vasarely, Jesús Rafael Soto

**Ambiguous figures** — **What:** Images interpreted two or more ways **How:** Brain can only hold one interpretation, so it “flips” **Artists:** Salvador Dalí, Octavio Ocampo, Sandro del Prete **Examples:** Young/old woman, vase/faces, duck/rabbit

steps.title: Create your own optical illusion
script: **Option A: Impossible Triangle** (Recommended for beginners) — Walk through step-by-step on board.
**Option B: Op Art Pattern** — Draw grid, systematically distort, fill alternating sections black.
**Option C: Ambiguous Figure** — Design image that can be seen two ways (advanced).
Circulate and assist. Encourage students to test illusions on classmates: *“Does it trick their eyes?”*

steps.title: The science behind the art
script: *“Every optical illusion you created today works because you understand something about how the brain processes visual information. Artists like Escher and Riley weren’t just making pretty pictures—they were exploring the limits of human perception.”*
**Reflection questions:** *“Which technique was most challenging? Why?”* / *“What did you learn about how your brain sees?”* / *“How might you use these techniques in other artwork?”*
